Varun Beverages Limited
Q3 & 9M CY2026 Earnings Conference Call Transcript
October 30, 2026
Moderator: Ladies and gentlemen, good day, and welcome to Varun Beverages Limited's
Earnings Conference Call.
I now hand the conference over to Mr. Anoop Poojari from CDR India. Thank you,
and over to you, Mr. Poojari.
Anoop Poojari: Thank you. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us on Varun
Beverages Q3 CY2026 earnings conference call. We have with us Mr. Varun
Jaipuria, Executive Vice Chairman and Whole-Time Director, and Mr. Raj Gandhi,
President and Whole-Time Director of the company. Mr. Ravi Jaipuria, Chairman of
the company, has had to excuse himself from today's call due to personal reasons.
We will begin the call with opening remarks from the management, following which
we will have the forum open for a question-and-answer session. Before we proceed,
I would like to point out that some statements made in today's call may be forward-
looking in nature, and a disclaimer to this effect has been included in the results
presentation shared with you earlier.
I will now request Mr. Varun Jaipuria to make his opening remarks.
Varun Jaipuria: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us on our earnings conference
call. I hope you have had a good chance to review our results presentation for the
third quarter and nine months ended September 30, 2026.
We are pleased to report a strong performance in the third quarter of CY2026.
Consolidated sales volume revenue grew 28.7% with a volume growth of 22.5% in
India and 39.9% in international markets. Revenue from operations increased by
33.2% year-on-year to Rs. 66,075.6 million, while EBITDA grew 25.1% to Rs.
14,267.1 million. Higher packaging costs weighed on margins during the quarter,
Page 1 of 21

although improved realizations and operating leverage from strong volume growth
helped partially offset these pressures.
In India, we continue to witness healthy volume growth during the quarter, extending
the positive trend seen since May. This performance was supported by our extensive
distribution network, expanded manufacturing capacities and ongoing investments
in chilling infrastructure. We also saw improved realizations supported by growth in
higher-value categories such as dairy and the introduction of premium offerings
including ‘Ad Rush’ and the ‘Evervess’ mixers range.
Our international business continued to make strong progress during the quarter with
Africa remaining a key continent for expansion. With effect from 1st August 2026,
the merger of Twizza with BevCo has been completed, and we expect to unlock
significant operational synergies in the coming quarters. During the quarter, we have
also started beverage operations in Kenya and introduced two new beverage brands,
‘BOLT UP’ and ‘XTREME FIZZ’, marking another step towards strengthening our
footprint in the fast-growing African region. We also entered into an exclusive
distribution agreement with Mondelez in Zimbabwe, further broadening our product
offering in the market.
We are also taking measured steps towards diversifying our business into adjacent
categories. The incorporation of KIVA Spirits and Company Limited marks an
important step in exploring opportunities in ready-to-drink beverages, alcoholic
beverages and allied products. Our approach will remain focused on pursuing
opportunities that leverage our execution capabilities and offer attractive long-term
growth potential.
In line with our dividend policy, the Board of Directors have approved an interim
dividend of 25% of the face value, Rs. 0.50 per share, resulting in total cash outflow
of Rs. 1,691 million.
Looking ahead, our focus will remain on driving growth across our existing markets,
supported by investments we have already made over the recent years. Alongside
this, we will selectively pursue opportunities to broaden our business while
maintaining a clear emphasis on profitability and long-term value creation.
I would now like to invite Mr. Gandhi to share the key highlights of our operational
and financial performance. Thank you.
Page 2 of 21

Raj Gandhi: Thank you, Mr. Vice Chairman. Good afternoon, and a warm welcome to everyone
joining us today. Let me take you through the financial and operational performance
of the third quarter and nine months ended 30th September 2026.
Revenue from operations net of excise duty and GST increased by 33.2% year-on-
year to the level of Rs. 66,076 million in Q3 CY2026. For 9M CY2026, revenue grew
by 23.3% to the level of Rs. 218,146 million. Growth during the quarter was primarily
driven by a 28.7% increase in consolidated sales volume to the level of 354.4 million
cases in India. Volume grew by a strong 22.5% during the quarter, while international
territories recorded robust growth of 39.9%.
Consolidated net realization per case for beverages improved by 2.2% year-on-year,
supported by a 0.5% increase in India on account of growth in high-value categories
and further launch of premium categories like Ad Rush, Evervess mixers range,
calibrated discounting and efficient price-pack architecture.
In international markets, realization per case improved on account of improved
realization in South Africa and foreign exchange impact. In terms of volume mix,
carbonated soft drinks accounted for 73.3%, juice-based drinks for 4.8% and
packaged drinking water for 21.9% of total sales volume during the quarter.
Coming to margins, gross margin moderated by 334 basis points year-on-year to
53.1% in Q3 calendar year 2026, primarily due to higher packaging material costs,
including preforms, shrink films, closures, cans, arising from geopolitical disruptions.
However, packaging cost contributed approximately 300 bps of pressure on gross
margin. In addition, sales of non-beverage products such as preforms and caps in
India increased by approximately 104% during the quarter. Given their higher COGS,
these products had an impact of approximately 100 basis points on gross margin in
India.
The impact of around a 16% increase in sugar price was largely offset by a higher
proportion of low sugar and no sugar products in India with their share increasing
from 44% levels in the corresponding Q3 of 2025 to the level of 88% in the Q3 of the
2026 in India, almost double. This is after accounting for the sharing of sugar
reduction benefits with PepsiCo through concentrate cost as part of the transition to
a low sugar portfolio.
EBITDA increased by 25.1% year-on-year to the level of Rs. 14,267 million in Q3
CY2026 with EBITDA margin at 21.6%. The margin moderated only by 140 basis
points in spite of higher material costs year-on-year, primarily due to the contraction
in gross margin, primarily offset by operating leverage from robust volume growth
Page 3 of 21

across India and international territories. Importantly, despite the supply chain
disruptions and input cost pressures arising from geopolitical developments, EBITDA
margins in India remained broadly stable on a year-to-year basis during 9M CY2026.
PAT increased by 13.5% year-on-year to the level of Rs. 8,306 million in Q3 CY2026,
compared with the Rs. 7,315 million in the corresponding quarter last year.
Depreciation and finance costs increased by 34.5% and 53.5%, respectively,
primarily on account of acquisition of Twizza in South Africa and the associated debt
funding. Other income declined by 18.8%, reflecting relatively stable currency
movements during the quarter.
For 9M CY2026, EBITDA increased by 19.9% to the level of Rs. 52,746 million, while
PAT grew up by 15.5% to Rs. 32,023 million.
Looking ahead, we are encouraged by the strong volume growth, delivered across
India and international markets. Our endeavor will be to sustain healthy growth over
the longer term, supported by effective utilization of our expanded capacities and
market infrastructure. At the same time, we will remain focused on managing input
costs and improving operating efficiencies to support profitability as we scale our
operations.
On that note, I will come to an end of our opening remarks and would like to now ask
the moderator to open the forum for any questions or suggestions that you may have.
Thank you.
Moderator: Thank you very much, sir. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin with the
question-and-answer session. The first question is from the line of Abneesh Roy from
Nuvama. Please go ahead.
Abneesh Roy: Thanks and congrats on strong volume growth in India and overseas also. My first
question is on the gross margins. What will be the outlook for next quarter and if
possible, even the March quarter? And coming specifically to this quarter, earlier the
information sharing was that sugar that change has happened. So very low sugar
usage is there in terms of the portfolio, plus in terms of the packaging, a lot of the
buying has been done for the September quarter. I wanted to understand where
things change versus that initial comment. And on your specific comment that non-
beverage has grown very sharply, preforms, caps, etc. So what is the reason for
that? And could you bifurcate how much is the packaging increase, sugar increase
and this non-beverage increase? That can give us more clarity. Thank you.
Page 4 of 21

Raj Gandhi: Abneesh, in the opening remarks, we clarified that food costs have not had a
significant impact due to the change in our portfolio and innovation. The share of low-
sugar or no-sugar products has increased from 44% to 88%, which has been
managed very well. However, due to geopolitical factors, packaging costs have
increased. Your comment is correct, but that was relevant only until the war started,
around 28th February. At that time, we had stated that we were fully covered for the
next quarter. As you might have noticed, there was no impact on gross margins last
quarter.
However, all purchases going forward were at higher prices. We had not stocked
inventory for a period longer than the 2nd quarter, which helped us manage the
previous quarters. However, prices are now definitely higher.
Abneesh Roy: And how do we see outlook?
Raj Gandhi: Outlook, this is a macro factor impacting both food and packaging costs. However,
in our case, through innovation, we have been able to manage sugar costs quite
well. As far as material costs are concerned, it may not be possible to comment
specifically.
However, in terms of mitigating the 3%-4% impact in gross margins, we have already
mitigated more than half of it through cost reductions.
Varun Jaipuria: Abneesh, looking at the geopolitical situation, nobody really knows when this war is
going to end and what is going to happen with the fuel prices. Now the question is
that the industry for two quarters has been feeling the pain of the cost going up
because of the raw material cost is increasing. We think there is enough chatter
within the Beverage Industry, which is all the players who are there in terms of if the
prices do remain high, then what are the measures they will take? Because over two
quarters, we usually do not act so fast on price-pack architecture. But there is
conversation if the pricing stays high, do they downsize certain packs, do they take
certain pricing up or will there be a trade margin reduction. So we will have to wait
and see what happens on that.
Raj Gandhi: Abneesh, just to add to what Mr. Varun Jaipuria stated, we have already reduced the
pack size of Sting from 300 ml to 250 ml. So, depending upon the market condition,
competitive scenario, etc., the other products in the portfolio will also be reviewed
from time to time.
Abneesh Roy: Thanks. Just one quick follow-up. So this is extreme geopolitical situation, which
comes, say, once in 10 years and 20 years. And generally, Pepsi is known to have
Page 5 of 21

discussion on how they can help here, especially given the new Cola player has an
in-house, obviously, one of the largest PET supply, so they can absorb this cost while
you and the other legacy players will have to face that. So any talks with Pepsi to
handhold in this scenario?
Varun Jaipuria: We think it is too early. We are all figuring out what price pack can we do. Of course,
cost is increasing, not just for us. We are sure for PepsiCo as well, the back-end cost
must be increasing. Hence, for the industry, the cost is increasing. So we are going
to wait and watch. If you look at this quarter, we have done fairly very well in terms
of volume and negating the 400 basis points of cost increase. Now going forward, if
we believe that we are not going to be able to negate it, then of course, the whole
industry will take some action on price pack for sure to negate it.
Abneesh Roy: Sure. Second and last question on this Mondelez relationship in Africa in Zimbabwe.
Any numbers you can share from a longer term, 3-5 years, what can be the
opportunity here? And do you see more markets getting added, adjacent markets in
Africa from Mondelez?
Varun Jaipuria: It is very nascent. Mondelez is one of the best brands you can work with. And we are
very fortunate to partner up with them. They already have an existing business of
about $11 million in Zimbabwe with the local partner they were working with, We are
sure he was not able to harness the full potential of the market. Hence, we are
partnering up with them. We do understand Zimbabwe very well, it was a greenfield
project for us a few years back. At present, we have got a very high market share
there and the volumes are growing. With Mondelez we are getting the whole portfolio
for distribution, and we are quite hopeful once we understand what the whole market
is and once we start the distribution properly, we can come back to you and give you
some concrete answers on it.
Moderator: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Vivek Maheshwari from Jefferies.
Please go ahead.
Vivek Maheshwari: Hi, good afternoon. A couple of questions. First is on the competition side. You know,
we have had one of the food companies, which did mention that the competition
seems to be abating right now. What are your thoughts on the same issue, please?
Varun Jaipuria: Sorry, what is your question on the competition exactly?
Vivek Maheshwari: So what I am saying is like Tata Consumer on their conference call mentioned that
they sounded far more confident on the market structure and how things are
Page 6 of 21

evolving. What is your view on the competition in general, your latest thoughts,
please?
Varun Jaipuria: So, we think we had subdued quarters last year due to the seasonality as what we
had mentioned. If you see our quarter 1, we had performed very well, high double-
digit growth is what we had. And then quarter 2 due to unseasonal rains, obviously,
has gone down, which we had clarified earlier. Now again, the weather has been
very good. The price pack is holding up in the market. The growth is back. So there
is no reason why we believe that the growth should not be coming going forward.
And we mentioned many times that the per caps in India are still very low right now
compared to even our neighbouring countries and the amount of expansion of
growth, which is there even for us and our competition today, we all can grow. Hence,
if you see today, even if we have grown, We are sure all our competitors are growing,
even Tata Consumer has given very good numbers is what we hear in terms of their
beverage portfolio. So there is no reason as to why we should all not keep growing.
Vivek Maheshwari: Got it. The other thing, Varun, when I look at your India unit realizations, in the last
6-7 quarters, there has been a downward pressure, and we saw that changing in
early part of this year, and then we have seen further buildup from there.
I know the raw material trend has been difficult, which is why you explained about
the price and the mix and everything. But does that also signal that like December
last year, the unit realization was at the bottom, the worst from a competition
standpoint, does that also signal from this unit realization in India trend?
Raj Gandhi: Vivek, instead of giving a forward statement, we draw your attention to look at this
quarter, that trend is already reversed and there is increase in realization per case.
We think that is a good indication, and you can build on that.
Varun Jaipuria: See, Vivek, one more thing to add. If you remove the raw material pressure, there is
so much operational efficiency what we have built in and there is so much operational
leverage because of growth what we are getting. And even if you see a 9M trend,
we are trailing at 16%-17% growth now largely, right, which is a good double-digit
growth. And we think there are a lot of initiatives what we have done internally as
well. It could be the mid-cal saving what we have brought in, bigger plant operation
is what we brought in, a lot of distributor consolidation is what we have done. So
these are routine things what we keep doing, which gives us huge operational
flexibility. Now we believe going forward, these are routine things which will keep
happening. So if the raw material element goes out and start stabilizing, We think
there should be no concerns when it comes to our margins.
Page 7 of 21

Vivek Maheshwari: Got it. And the second question is on the international business. Obviously, the
volume growth, both organically and reported basis has been very good. Given that
it is a geography or the cluster of geographies, which we do not fully understand, can
you just talk about your outlook from a next few quarter perspective on the
international side? And anything to call out for any of the geographies?
Varun Jaipuria: See, we are doing very well in Africa, in most of the places we are out of capacity.
We are investing in capex in Morocco now because we do not have enough capacity
there. We are investing in Zimbabwe since we do not have capacity. In DRC, we are
putting a line up as well. So, we have sold out in most of the places and the outlook
is very positive. There is enough and more room to grow in Africa. It is again, a very
nascent market. And if you see the last 4-6-8 quarters, there is tremendous growth
is what we are seeing, and that is continuing.
Vivek Maheshwari: Got it. And anything on the currency side of things because it has moved a bit, but
are there any concerns on that front in any of the markets?
Raj Gandhi: There is no worry, Vivek. The only thing is last year, local currencies had gone up
vis-a-vis dollar. This year, this has stabilized. There are a lot of commodities,
minerals, metals and other natural resources, which are in demand and because of
which those African currencies are holding on. In fact, the South African currency
has become costlier since we acquired BevCo and Twizza.
Vivek Maheshwari: Got it. And Mr. Gandhi, last thing, which is in the earlier quarter, you had mentioned
about there was some impact of regulatory issues on the energy drink in, I think,
June as well as if I recall correctly, you mentioned for July. How things are on the
energy drink side in this quarter?
Varun Jaipuria: So, the energy is coming back. I am sure you are aware of the whole issue, which
happened with FSSAI that they had banned the use of the word energy on labels.
Because the registration for most energy brands in India was done under carbonated
beverages, not under energy as a category, because energy as a category did not
exist in India. So the ruling what they had was you cannot use energy. Of course,
that created some turmoil in the market amongst the retailers and the distributors.
But we think that is for everybody, and we see Sting holding a very high market share
in the energy segment. So, Sting is coming back. The volumes are looking promising,
and it is building back.
Vivek Maheshwari: Got it. Would you be able to quantify where it is today versus if 100 is the baseline?
Because the growth that we have seen, your commentary or comment suggests that
Page 8 of 21

it is still not up to the mark. So is that a fair understanding, which means the rest of
the portfolio growth has been faster than what the headline numbers suggest then?
Varun Jaipuria: No, of course, that has to be there. Because in the middle, people were not sure if
they want to stock up energy or not from every distributor, not just us, competitor
products and retailers are not sure if they want to stock up energy. So let us assume
the negativity was 25%. Now we can say we are slightly positive. So I think month-
on-month on a quarter, we are moving towards a positive range versus where we
were at least. So that puts it in the right context for you.
Moderator: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Aditya Soman from CLSA. Please
go ahead.
Aditya Soman: Hi. Good afternoon. Sir, two questions from me. Firstly, can you give us a sense of
the volume growth that you are seeing for the noncarbonated business? And second,
you indicated that you have taken a price increase or volume cut for Sting. When
was this taken? And broadly, the price increase that we are seeing in the portfolio as
well for India from a timing perspective, should we expect that to play out fully in the
December quarter?
Varun Jaipuria: There is no pricing which we have taken on the CSD portfolio, that has come through
operational efficiency that we had mentioned. And the consolidation of distributors
and bigger plant productions, more operational efficiency, mid-cal sugar savings,
some saving in trade spends we did. So there is no pricing on the CSD portfolio or
there is no change in the pack size what we have done this quarter. On Sting, the
downsize what we did from 300 ml to 250 ml. I think it was May or June, around
about that time.
Moderator: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Devanshu Bansal from Emkay
Global. Please go ahead.
Devanshu Bansal: Hi, Varun. Thanks for the opportunity and congratulations on the very strong
domestic volume growth. Varun, my question is to better understand how
unorganized industry is playing out, right? So while the margin is a hit for us, but it is
a bigger hit for the smaller unorganized players. We have preserved our magic price
points. So I wanted to check if this can lead to better growth for us in the coming
quarter or next year. So any views if you could share?
Varun Jaipuria: See, the example we give everybody is if you go to the southern markets, the industry
mix in the southern market is almost 50% B-brands, whereas if you come to the
northern markets, only probably 15%-18%. But if you go there, as per us, we are
Page 9 of 21

growing, and they are also growing. So there is a different market and different
consumer who is consuming our price points versus the Rs. 10 plus price points.
Now of course, the margin pressures are high. Our water growth are better because
water is where the most amount of pressure is for B-brands and local players due to
the increase in availability and the increase in raw material cost. So I think they are
growing, we do not have an exact number, and we are looking at a good double-digit
growth in terms of what we have delivered.
Devanshu Bansal: So my question was more from our growth perspective. So can this turbulent period
lead to better growth for us? Because we are not changing our price points. So can
we grow faster versus what we were expecting earlier?
Varun Jaipuria: See, my only question is when they are selling full sugar at Rs. 10, we are not sure
how B-brands are able to sell. We have no idea how they are running their business
or what they are doing. We cannot answer that. We know that our growth are coming
20% plus, which we are very happy about. And we are hoping we can deliver better
numbers.
Devanshu Bansal: I am saying PET is ballpark 10%-15% of your sales. We have indicated a 300 basis
points margin impact, which says the raw material increase is only 20%-30%, right?
But if you see crude prices, they are up like 50%-odd. So I wanted to check if this
entire crude increase is baked in the current P&L or we may see some more sort of
impact as we go down the line?
Raj Gandhi: The 100% impact of crude price is already built in because all these fresh stocks are
being consumed. And the prices, of course, depend on when we time the purchases,
which helps us. And, if you remember, we had invested in rPET. With rPET as a
backward integration, we have in-house rPET supplies. Around 25% is our rPET,
which is much cheaper than the virgin PET and that has helped us to keep this pricing
under control.
And yes, we have the cost advantage. And if it is ploughed back in the market,
definitely, it can also help in increasing the share. But as Mr. Varun Jaipuria said, we
are happy with 20-plus percentage growth. And if any upside to that comes, we will
share.
Varun Jaipuria: We welcome it happily.
Moderator: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Anand Shah from Axis Capital.
Please go ahead.
Page 10 of 21

Anand Shah: Hi team. Just a couple of questions here. Firstly, I mean, anything you can share on
this expansion on existing categories and especially KIVA. I mean it is early days,
but what kind of capital deployment you are looking at and what kind of plans?
Varun Jaipuria: Its very early days. We think Alcobev is an interesting space to get into, especially
RTDs, the way they are growing in India and we think there is huge scope to grow
them in Africa as well. RTDs, if you see, they are growing at about 13%-15% and
we are looking where we can partner up and get into RTDs. That is the first thing.
Secondly, even global brands like PepsiCo, all the other guys, they have entered
RTD in the U.S., U.K. and Canada with their core brands, which is Pepsi, Mountain
Dew, 7UP because that is what the younger generation is drinking now. Our plans
are to enter RTD right now. That is the first thing. We are also looking, which we are
in talks with right now with a lot of global players to partner up and bring to India.
See, our idea in alcohol is largely going to do the portfolio, we would like to play the
Prestige plus. So we are not looking at margin dilutive portfolios. If we can maintain
higher margins, work with international brands, get the right brand and premiumize
the portfolio. So it is still a lot of things work in play. And hopefully, in the next call,
we will be able to give you more clarity.
Anand Shah: Got it. And here, you will be open to inorganic as well?
Varun Jaipuria: Of course.
Anand Shah: Got it. And lastly, you did call out a little bit of impact on Sting in the interim and now
it is coming back. I mean, so while you have some volume impact, it would have also
had realization impact, right? I mean, given its higher realizations versus the other
portfolio?
Varun Jaipuria: Yes, however, it got nullified as well because we had a 300 ml earlier since COGS
have gone up, and we did downsize to 250 ml. So there has been obviously some
negation of the raw material impact when we did downsize.
Anand Shah: Got it. And beyond Sting, any other price pack architecture changes you have done,
I mean, like from 300ml to 250 ml, anything that you want to?
Varun Jaipuria: No, not as yet. This year which was very important for us was to just maintain and
make sure that we get into the high double-digit growth. And a lot of pack price
intervention, which we had done were looking at how dynamic the market was. In
the earlier question, Vivek or Abneesh has asked, that how it looks going forward
with all the raw material pressures. So we are going to see what the industry does,
Page 11 of 21

and it is a rapidly fast-moving industry. It is not like it was earlier, and we are on our
toes as well. And our job is to make sure we can maintain our margin as best as we
can and offset the costs as much as we can. And we think we have done a good job
this quarter. And hopefully, going forward, we will plan in terms of how the industry
moves.
Anand Shah: Got it. Fairly clear. And just very last, anything you want to call out on October as
well? I mean you are seeing similar momentum sort of continue?
Raj Gandhi: Quarter is still in progress, Anand. We think we should wait.
Moderator: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Arnab Mitra from Goldman Sachs.
Please go ahead.
Arnab Mitra: Hi, thanks for the opportunity. My first question was on the Africa business. If you
could just let us know the constant currency growth and how much was the currency
benefit on the top line? And a related question is that as you go into the season in
Africa, which is December quarter, March quarter, given the capacity situation, do
you think the volume growth can taper off from these very high levels? Or do you
think you have enough capacities to be able to sustain growth even in the season in
Africa?
Raj Gandhi: See, there are two questions. One is about currency. This year, we said that the
currency is more stable. So, there is no effect. If there is anything marginal, it gets
compensated across one country and another. Last year, yes, we called out there
was a good benefit of the currency, which we had duly accounted for.
And the second question is about the capacity. We are preparing ourselves fully
because the season in South Africa and DRC is November, December and January.
And there, we are already running our plants at full speed. And Morocco, where the
season was in August where the capacity is short. And hopefully, before the next
season, we will have enough capacity installed at all locations.
As far as South Africa is concerned, with the Twizza acquisition, we have enough
capacity. And we do not think we will face a shortage this year. The only little bit of a
gap was found in Zimbabwe, where Zambia had overcapacity, and we will be
supporting Zimbabwe from there from this month itself.
Varun Jaipuria: And for next year, we are anyway adding more capacity in Zimbabwe as well.
Arnab Mitra: Got it. My second question was on international business margins. So it seems to
have held up better than the standalone in terms of gross margin also. So one is,
Page 12 of 21

has it been easier to pass pricing there? Or is it more to do with your own initiatives
on backward integration? And therefore, will the margins be better protected there
because they would also have the same inflationary pressures?
Raj Gandhi: See, the margin is slightly improved because Twizza has the backward integration
and we have started similar initiatives in other places as well. So the improvement in
margins is because of that. And rest is due to the economies of scale, which have
started playing in. And in the opening remarks, as we stated, Twizza was effectively
integrated into BevCo from 1st August 2026. So a lot of synergies there have already
started showing up.
Arnab Mitra: Just one quick follow-up. So the input cost pressure on PET and cans and all, they
are fully reflecting in September quarter, even in the international business?
Raj Gandhi: In international, this is 272 basis points as against around 300 basis points in India.
India is looking slightly higher.
Varun Jaipuria: But it is all been accounted for in the quarter.
Moderator: Thank you. The next question is from the line of Jay Doshi from Kotak Securities.

Jay Doshi: Hi. Thanks. Thanks for the opportunity. I have a few questions. First one on
